{{Short description|German physicist and entrepreneur}}
'''Günther Laukien''' (23 May 1923, in [[Eschringen]] ([[Saarland]]) – 29 April 1997, in [[Karlsruhe]]) was a German [[physicist]] and [[entrepreneur]]. He is known for his pioneering work in [[nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy]] and for his role in the [[Bruker]] company.

==Early life==
Laukien was born in 1924 in the [[Germany|German]] village of [[Eschringen]]<ref name="Ernst2005">{{cite journal|last1=Ernst|first1=Richard R.|title=The Günther Laukien Prize|journal=Journal of Magnetic Resonance|volume=173|issue=2|year=2005|pages=188–191|issn=1090-7807|doi=10.1016/j.jmr.2005.02.006|pmid=15780911}}</ref> in the [[Saarland]]. He finished [[high school]] in 1942 – during [[World War II]] – and joined the [[German Navy]] as a [[submarine]] engineer after his graduation. After the war ended in 1945, he studied [[physics]] at the [[University of Tübingen]], from which he received his [[undergraduate degree]] in 1951.

==Academic career==
In 1955 he graduated on the "experimental aspects of nuclear magnetic resonance" at the [[University of Stuttgart]]. This was done under professor [[Hans Otto Kneser]].<ref name="Ernst2005"/> He wrote his doctoral thesis on "Freie Präzession kernmagnetischer Momente" (''Free precession of [[nuclear magnetic moment]]s'').<ref>G. Laukien, PhD Thesis, Freie Präzession kernmagnetischer
Momente, Universität Stuttgart, 1955.</ref> His thesis already explored the techniques behind [[nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy]], at a time when this was not developed yet. Only a couple of earlier papers had explored this subject, and Laukien was most likely unknown with those papers.<ref>R. Gabillard, Mesure du temps de relaxation T2 en présence d’une inhomogénéité de champ magnétique supérieure à la largeur de raie, Comptes Rendues 232 (1951) 1551–1553.</ref><ref>H.Y. Carr, PhD Thesis, Free precession techniques in nuclear magnetic resonance, Harvard University, 1952.</ref> After getting his [[PhD]], he became "Oberassistent"<!--Assistent professor?--> and in 1957 he achieved [[habilitation]]. In 1958 he moved from Stuttgart to the [[University of Karlsruhe]], where he became a [[professor]] in 1960. In 1968 he became a life-time professor in electronics at [[Ruhr University Bochum]]<ref name="Ernst2005"/> In 1980 Günther Laukien received the ISMAR prize, which is awarded for outstanding achievement in the field of magnetic resonance.<ref name="Ernst2005"/> In 2013 he posthumously received the [[Pittcon Heritage Award]] for his contributions to the development of nuclear magnetic resonance and other analytical technologies.<ref name="Pittcon">{{cite web|title=Pittcon Heritage Award|url=https://www.sciencehistory.org/pittcon-heritage-award|website=[[Science History Institute]]|accessdate=23 March 2018}}</ref>

==Bruker==
In 1960 he co-founded and soon chaired the [[Bruker]] spectroscopy company (then named ''Bruker-Physik AG''), which was specialized in designing and using [[electromagnets]], with applications in [[nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy]]. Until his death, Laukien was actively involved in both research and business aspects of the company.<ref name="Ernst2005"/>

==Personal life==
Laukien had four sons who were all involved in [[Bruker]].<ref name="cashes-out">{{cite web|url=http://www.bizjournals.com/boston/stories/2009/06/01/daily53.html|title=Insider report: Bruker cashes out Laukiens|date=1 June 2009}}</ref> 

Developing underwater equipment was one of his hobbies.<ref>{{cite journal|journal=Izvestiya Akademii Nauk SSSR. Seriya Khimicheskaya|title=Günter Laukin (to his 70th birthday)|volume=43|number=5|year=1994}}</ref> 

He died in 1997 of [[cancer]], aged 73.{{cn|date=June 2023}}
